Three success edits shared an anchor with a failure edit, so I re-anchored them to avoid insertion-order ambiguity, since the failure edits keep their original anchors. S1 (puns/wordplay and ignoring framing, support 2) now follows the Rule 1 'Always output the specific entity...' sentence, and the failure edit about name-and-title and parenthetical clues keeps the 'context passages usually reveal the link' anchor. S6 (co-subject and parody clues, support 2) now follows the 'One of these <role/title>' bullet, so it sits next to the failure edit about possessives, 'she/he' and events. edits.target: Other named entities in the clue are anchors, never the answer.
edits.content:
- A possessive pronoun ('his', 'her', 'their'), 'she / he / this actor / this man / this woman' next to a named event, treaty, battle, book, or a list of roles or works means the answer is the PERSON behind it, never the thing named in the clue or listed in the passages: 'The 1815 Treaty of Paris was signed after his final defeat at Waterloo' -> 'Napoleon', not 'Treaty of Paris'; 'played Tina Turner on screen & Rosa Parks on TV' -> 'Angela Bassett' (the name recurring in the passages), not a film or show title. Sanity check: if your answer repeats the clue's own distinctive words, it is probably wrong.
- If the clue already supplies a branch, campus, city or qualifier ('this state university at Superior, not Madison'), the answer is the base/parent name without it ('University of Wisconsin', not 'University of Wisconsin-Superior').

edits.target: The context passages about the topic usually reveal the link.
edits.content:
- A clue that is only a person's name and title ('Sultan Haji Hassanal Bolkiah') is a category-style clue. Answer with the country, realm or organization the passages tie him to, in bare form ('Brunei', not 'Sultan of Brunei').
- A parenthetical identifier in the clue ('seen here: (U.S. president, '81-'89)') describes the answer, which here is the person who fits it ('Ronald Reagan'). When the clue refers to an unseen picture, ignore that part and answer from the description. Archive pages list many clues one after another, so never take the answer from a neighbouring clue ('Starr' came from the preceding clue).

edits.target: Always output the specific entity, word, or name that the clue is asking for.
edits.content:
- Puns and wordplay in the clue ('no flash in the Tai-Pan', 'a hot ticket') are decoration. Find the plain factual core ('author of Gai-Jin') and answer that. Title words and jargon in the clue are anchors. Jargon that fits only one thing ('doux ... brut', 'Bharat Ratna') points to that thing (Champagne, India), even if the passages only mention it in glossaries.
- Ignore framing that is not part of the fact: a leading parenthetical such as '(Jimmy of the Clue Crew at the St. James Theatre...)', or pointers to unseen media such as 'whose flag is seen here'. Answer from the remaining descriptors ('troubled Mediterranean island nation' -> Cyprus). Never say the image or video is missing.

edits.target: - Otherwise, build the answer from passages that match several of the clue's details.
edits.content: - Read the passage titles ([TLE] headings such as 'Cyprus - Wikipedia', 'Bullfighting - Wikipedia', 'The King and I - Wikipedia'). When several top passages are titled around, or keep repeating, one entity that also matches the clue's descriptors, that entity is very likely the answer. Confirm it is the right TYPE for the slot (Rule 2), then answer it directly without overthinking.

edits.target: Take the answer that follows the clue, even if the whole context is one short passage.
edits.content: - Definition-style clues ('A double that visually resembles another') want the term whose dictionary or thesaurus gloss matches the clue almost word for word. A thesaurus line like 'noun someone closely resembling another' -> 'look-alike'. Do not answer with a narrower or merely related term ('Body double'), and do not add a qualifier. For 'this type/kind of X' clues, answer with the named variety that a passage ties to the clue's detail ('I knew they put rubber in bubble gum' -> 'bubble gum'). Keep its normal compound name. Do not answer with an adjective describing the material or composition ('synthetic').

edits.target: Do not talk yourself out of a well-supported entity.
edits.content: - If one passage holds only the clue's own wording cut off before the answer (e.g. a flashcard 'IT'S THE SPANISH NAME FOR A POPULAR PARTY DRINK MADE WITH RED WINE...'), the answer is the entity that the other passages DEFINE with those same descriptors ('made with red wine, fruit juices' -> Sangria). It is not a neighbouring entity that is mentioned only in passing or differs on one descriptor (Agua de Valencia). Count how often each candidate is tied to ALL the clue's descriptors, and take the most frequent one.

edits.target: e.g. 'The New York Times', 'The Divine Comedy').
edits.content: - Strip descriptor words only when they are NOT part of the entity's standard name. Keep generic words that belong to a proper name: a clue about 'this 1337-1453 conflict' -> 'Hundred Years' War' (not 'Hundred Years'); 'this book' -> 'Great Expectations'; 'this miniseries' -> 'The Stand'. Test: would the answer key list the entity with that word? If yes, keep it.

edits.target: Still apply the person-name rule above.
edits.content: - The reverse case: when the clue gives the real name and asks for the person's 'moniker / nickname / better-known name / alias' ('William Marcy Tweed's better known moniker'), answer with only the nickname as the passages repeat it, in its shortest standard form ('Boss'). Do not return the real name, and do not add the surname unless the clue asks for the full alias.

- Modifiers in front of 'this' belong to the clue, not the answer: 'a miniature this' -> 'pizza' (not 'mini pizza'), 'this classic toy' -> 'Slinky', 'this country's award' -> 'India'. When the passages repeatedly name one entity that fits all the clue's details, answer it directly and do not second-guess it.

edits.target: do not append that role word to the answer.
edits.content:
- Blank that is one half of a '&' pair under a category such as 'Publishing partners', 'Duos', 'Law firms' or 'Comedy teams' ('___ & Wagnalls'): the category asks for the whole pair, so give the full name as written ('Funk & Wagnalls'). For a blank that is a single missing word inside an ordinary phrase, give only that word.
- Do not add generic tail words ('power', 'energy', 'system') that the clue's own noun already supplies after the slot ('a plant for this' -> 'hydroelectric', not 'hydroelectric power').

edits.target: - Ask: what category is the answer (country, person, vitamin, object, band), and what member of that category fits all the clue details?
edits.content:
- 'These' / 'those' with named examples: the answer is the category noun that the examples belong to. 'A series on these of the '30s & '40s features the Daylight & the 20th Century Limited' -> 'Trains', not the series or product name ('All Aboard! stamps').
- A clue that is only a descriptor plus a quoted title ('A 1961 classic: "West Side Story"') asks for something CONNECTED to that title, such as the source work it adapts, its author or its star. It never asks for the quoted title itself. Find the related entity the passages state next to the title ('a modern retelling of Shakespeare's Romeo and Juliet') and answer with it.

edits.target: asks for the title or category noun itself (Dalai Lama), not the individual named in the clue.
edits.content:
- Co-subject clues ('Lemmon & this actor joined an all-girl band', 'X and this man ...'): the person already named is given. The answer is the OTHER participant the passages list alongside him (Tony Curtis), never the named one.
- Parody, spoof or disguised-name clues ('A Bret Harte tale parodied this detective as Hemlock Jones'): the altered name in the clue is only an anchor. The answer is the original figure or work being parodied ('Sherlock Holmes'), in its full, standard name.

edits.target: let the unique detail win (Khartoum -> Sudan even if Sudan is no longer 'largest').
edits.content: - Unique details include distances, dates, capital/largest status, and foreign-language terms in quotes. A passage's own subject can be a nearby or related entity rather than the answer. Examples: the oil strike at Leduc No. 1 is not the answer when the clue says 'city 175 miles north of Calgary' and 'oil capital' (Edmonton); a passage saying 'futbol is most popular in Mexico' is not the answer when the clue says 'known as "corrida de toros"' (bullfighting). Choose the entity that satisfies the unique detail.

edits.target: - Honor qualifiers when the context offers several names for the same thing: 'Greek god of erotic love' -> 'Eros' (not Roman 'Cupid').
edits.content:
- Abbreviation-letter clues ('The second "S" in LSUS stands for this city'): find the full expanded name in the passages ('LSU Shreveport') and answer the word that letter stands for ('Shreveport'). Do not answer with the place most associated with the main part of the abbreviation (Baton Rouge for LSU).
- Time words in a clue ('current', 'present', 'new', 'latest') reflect when the clue was written, often decades ago. Pick the entity whose concrete facts (schooling, deeds, dates) match the clue, even if a later holder of the title exists: 'This current king of Jordan ... Harrow & Sandhurst' -> 'King Hussein' (the passages' form), not Abdullah II.
- Answer with the base common name, without added qualifiers such as 'sea', 'common' or 'American', unless the clue itself includes them: 'lamprey', not 'sea lamprey'.
